resumen: Lines, frames and patience for the street, and how to look after the lights at night.

bloques.alt: A street in perspective. The edges of the sidewalk and the building fronts form lines that lead the eye to the back: 1, leading lines. On one side, a door acts as a frame: 2, frame. In the middle, a small person walks through a pool of light: 3, pool of light.
bloques.pie: Street in perspective. 1 Leading lines. 2 Frame: a door or a window. 3 Pool of light: wait for someone to step in.

bloques.texto: In the street you can't arrange anything: pick the setting, wait for life to pass through it and shoot fast. At night, protect the lights.

Look for [[lineas-guia|leading lines]]: a street, a railing or the shadow of a building that lead the eye to your subject. Also look for a natural frame, like a door or a window. Puddles and shiny surfaces give reflections.
Pick a background you like and wait for someone to walk through it.

You don't have to avoid harsh sun: its strong shadows can be the subject of the photo. A pool of light between buildings sets off whoever walks through it, and in the [[hora-dorada|golden hour]] the light is softer and warmer. Use a [[velocidad|shutter speed]] of 1/200 s or faster so that someone walking comes out sharp, and a middle [[apertura|aperture]], for example f/5.6 or f/8. In [[modo-av|Av or A]], watch that the shutter speed doesn't get longer.

bloques.alt: Two photos of the same street at night, with a street lamp. In the first, too bright, the lamp's light burns out: it is a white blob with no detail. In the second, with the brightness lowered, the lamp and its light show detail, and the dark parts stay dark.
bloques.pie: Too bright: the lights burn out. With the brightness lowered: the light shows detail and the dark parts stay dark.

bloques.texto: With strong lights and very dark areas, the lights tend to come out as white blobs with no detail.

items: Protect the lights: lower the exposure until you can see detail in the brightest part; the dark parts will stay dark. On a camera, with negative [[compensacion|exposure compensation]] (for example -1); on many phones, tap the strongest light and lower the brightness.
Better in the [[hora-azul|blue hour]]: the sky still has color and there is less difference between it and the lights.
Open the aperture as much as you can, raise the [[iso|ISO]] and, handheld, don't go below 1/100 s. With a tripod and a long shutter speed, cars leave trails of light.
Clean the lens and take off the UV filter: a smudge or a filter makes halos around lights.

bloques.texto: Not everyone likes being in a photo. If someone notices, be friendly; if they ask you to delete it, delete it. If a recognizable person is going to appear and you're going to publish the photo, the prudent thing is to ask permission; with children, be even more careful. Rules change from one country to another (in Spain, the law protects each person's image) and this is not legal advice.

It goes more unnoticed than a camera. To get closer, move closer yourself instead of pinching the screen, as in “Zoom and lenses”. At night, with night mode, stay still: anything that moves can come out blurry.

Pick a spot with street lamps. Take one photo and another with the brightness lowered, by tapping the strongest light, and compare. If a recognizable person appears and you're going to publish it, ask them first.
